newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss unveil bank list of possible holocaust victims.
newsitem.headline: Swiss unveil bank list of possible holocaust victims.

text.p: Swiss banks Tuesday unveiled a list of pre-1945 account holders who may have perished in the Holocaust, and invited their heirs to come forward.
Industry sources said the banks would also shortly announce they have found 40 percent more money in dormant accounts than they previously reported.

The list of some 2,000 account holders' names first appeared in early editions of Wednesday's Russian newspaper Izvestia, ahead of a Zurich news conference where it was to be presented in more detail.
Swiss banks are publishing the unprecedented three-page list in newspapers in 28 countries and on the Internet, breaking with a tradition of secrecy after criticism by Jewish groups.

Bankers who declined to be named said the total amount found in dormant accounts opened by foreigners before the end of World War Two was around 60 million Swiss francs ($40.5 million), rather than about 43 million as the banks said last year.
"It is about 60 million Swiss francs," said one banker familiar with the results of the search ordered by the Federal Banking Commission and reported to the Swiss Bankers Association.
The bankers association declined any immediate comment, and it was not immediately clear what may have caused the jump.

The association originally reported in February 1996 that a search undertaken by the banks came up with a provisional total of 39 million Swiss francs, then later raised that figure to around 43 million, spread between about 1,000 accounts.
The higher figure is likely to fuel suspicion by the World Jewish Congress (WJC) and its allies that Swiss banks have not revealed the true amount of Holocaust assets.

"Is it somewhere between 70 million and seven billion dollars? I don't know. But it certainly is far greater than the lowball figure given to us by the Swiss Bankers Association," WJC executive director Elan Steinberg told Reuters earlier.
The bankers group was due to release the new figures at a Zurich news conference Wednesday along with the list of account holders.
The long-awaited list names accounts opened by foreigners before 1945 and whose owners have not been heard from in at least 10 years.
These criteria mean the tally could include people who dropped out of contact for other reasons than the Holocaust.
The list as it appeared in Izvestia asked heirs, or people with information on account-holders, to contact the international accounting firm Ernst and Young.

"If you find a name you know on this list and you believe you are the lawful owner of an unidentified account or if you possess any information which may help find the real owner, please fill in the form," the Izvestia advert said in Russian.

"The process of reviewing claims is clear and simple. The whole procedure is free," the banks added. All rulings would be made within a year by independent arbiters and any unclaimed sums "from the time of the Holocaust" would go to charity.
They noted that some accounts were in multiple names and gave no figure for the amounts held.
The names ran from R. Joh. Aalberts in London to Dr. Karl G. Zwick in Cincinnati in the United States, followed by a shorter list of people holding proxy powers over dormant accounts.
Claimants can write or telephone Ernst and Young offices in New York (344-0610), Tel Aviv (623-2525), Basle (272-0811), Budapest (343-5117) or Sydney (9248-5736) for a free brochure.
In London, Jewish campaigners said the banks' decision was welcome but overdue.

"At last the Swiss are helping Holocaust survivors and victims of the Nazis and their families to recover money placed in Switzerland for safekeeping," Greville Janner of the Holocaust Educational Trust said in a statement.
"Their action now contrasts with the obstruction and evasion which greeted needy refugees who approached the banks for their money immediately after the war.
"If banks had ever seriously looked for owners then they would have saved years of suffering for thousands of people," he added.

The banks' advertisement said people could also check page www.dormantaccounts.ch on the World Wide Web, although an initial check showed this Internet page carrying a simple message that it would be updated Wednesday.

The list of names of foreigners will be followed in October by a second list detailing similar accounts opened by Swiss residents, who may have acted as proxies to hide away the assets of European Jews and others threatened by the Nazis.
